newsitem.title: USA: Star fund raiser Huang may turn star witness.
newsitem.headline: Star fund raiser Huang may turn star witness.

text.p: John Huang, a star fund-raiser for the Democratic party, may become the star witness in the Senate's probe of fund-raising scandals in the 1996 presidential election.

Huang, a former Commerce Department official who raised $3.4 million during his nine months with the Democratic National Committee, agreed Tuesday to testify before the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee if given limited immunity from prosecution.
Huang is at the crux of the investigation of campaign law violations and efforts by foreign governments to influence U.S. politics in the 1996 campaigns. He has refused to testify without immunity.

Through his attorney, Ty Cobb, Huang said he would waive immunity for any future prosecution for economic espionage, perjury, disclosure of classified information or laws on representation of foreign governments.

"Mr Huang is motivated not by fear of prosecution ... but instead by his passionate, even poignant, view that the interests of Asian Americans have suffered unduly because of his inability, under the circumstances, to respond," Cobb said in a letter to Sen. John Glenn. The Ohio Democrat is the senior member of his party on the panel.
Born in China in 1945 and raised in Taiwan, Huang became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 1976 and built ties to political and financial powerhouses on both sides of the Pacific.

Huang had a career in banking, including a stint in Hong Kong for the Memphis-based Union Planters' Bank. He was the top representative in Los Angeles for the Lippo Group, an Indonesian financial and real estate conglomerate owned by the Riady family, which is also under campaign finance scrutiny.

The Washington Post reported in Monday's editions that a real estate holding company run by Huang while he was with the Lippo Group allegedly was used to funnel money from Indonesia to U.S. election campaigns.
By 1994 he was a top international trade official in the Commerce Department run by the Ron Brown, the former head of the Democratic National Committee.

Huang organized large fund-raisers for Democrats, including one at a posh Washington hotel in February 1996 which netted $1.1 million. The DNC has returned almost half of what Huang raised and he was suspended after reports he solicited unlawful funds from a South Korean firm.
Senate Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Fred Thompson, a Tennessee Republican, and Glenn said immunity was under discussion.

"If Mr. Huang or anybody else wants to give full, complete and truthful information to the committee we are very much interested in it. If he has hatched a plan to absolve himself while at the same time covering for his friends we are not interested in that," Thompson said.
